name: Drabolve
lede: Drabolve is a dull, dark yellow-olive from Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary of color, filed by later standards as a moderate olive.

sections.title: An 1789 name on plate 15
sections.body: Maerz and Paul's 1930 *A Dictionary of Color* lists Drabolve on plate 15, swatch J5, and dates its first recorded use to 1789 [1]. That is one of the older dates on its plate, and the book does not explain what the name describes [1]. The National Bureau of Standards' 1955 circular, which cross-indexes the dictionary, places it inside the block it calls moderate olive, with a measured Munsell notation of 6.5Y 4.0/5.8 [2]. The nearest named colors on file are [[drabolve]], [[antique-bronze]], [[mud]] and [[metallic-green]], at 2.7, 3, 3.1 and 3.5 ΔE [2]. Drabolve sits further toward brown and further from green than plain olive, and [[brown]] on the same dull-yellow axis [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of Drabolve covers at least five percent of the canvas in 532 of them, about 2.2 percent overall, as photographed [3]. Its rate climbs through the nineteenth century and peaks in the 1830s, in 23 of 663 paintings, when it covers 5.1 percent of paintings, more than double the archive average [3]. Paulus Potter carries it most, in 9 of his 28 archived paintings, over fourteen times the average rate, and it most often keeps company with [[olive]] and [[khaki]] [3]. These are computed color matches on photographs of varnished paintings, not pigment identifications [3].
